item.title: U.S., Russia and Ukraine start talks aimed at ending war
item.description:
The United States, Ukraine and Russia have started talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday aimed at ending the war in Ukraine that began in 2022 when Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of his country's neighbor.
The two-day session is the first such meeting since February and will focus on security guarantees, a long-running demand from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said in a post on X that he and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were "working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."
Kushner indicated these talks are just an initial step but could "build momentum" toward future negotiations. He also suggested a future agreement would involve a security arrangement involving European countries and Russia.
Putin has previously said he wanted Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, the four regions Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demanded that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy rejected Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejected any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

item.title: Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sex assault
item.description:
Disgraced actor Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10 and a half years in prison for raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others.
The disgraced British television personality and Hollywood actor was convicted last week on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, but acquitted on two other counts of rape and an attempted indecent assault charge.
A jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court, in South London, found Brand guilty of groping a woman's breasts at a London bar in 2004, sexually assaulting a woman at a London radio station in 2004 and 2005, and raping a woman at his west London home in 2009.
The judge, Joel Bennathan, called Brand a "sexual predator" in his sentencing remarks, saying he displayed "staggering arrogance" and believed that "fame meant you could act ⁠how you liked, when you liked."
For the rape he was sentenced to nine years, plus 18 months for the sexual assaults. Brand is expected to serve at least seven years in prison, and the rest of his sentence under heavy restrictions, such as wearing a tag.
Six women made the allegations against him, spanning from 1999 to 2009.
Russell Brand outside Southwark Crown Court in London on Nov. 4, 2026.
James Manning/PA Images via Getty Images
Before the sentencing Monday, victim impact statements from the women involved in Brand's crimes were read out in court, three by the prosecutor and one by one of the women, who was hidden from everyone but the judge by a screen.
"I've been in shock and turmoil for years. I was extremely upset and traumatized. I didn't have any respect for myself," the woman reading her statement said, according to CBS News partner network BBC.

item.title: Trump says Iran war at "status quo," warns U.S. "locked and loaded"
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump said Monday the U.S. was keeping the Iran war at "status quo" but warned that American forces were "locked and loaded."In a 60 Minutes interview that aired Sunday, Mr. Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war. However, he defended starting the conflict as "historically" a good decision, despite its economic impact.Secretary of State Marco Rubio curbed expectations late Sunday, saying talks are not "at the verge of a breakthrough" because Iran's demands are "unacceptable."

item.title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
item.description:
French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks.
The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.
The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.
In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.
In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."
